<header class="editorial-hero"><div class="hero-main"><div class="hero-edition">Five interactive lessons · Net Promoter Score</div><h1>NPS under<br/>the microscope.</h1><p class="hero-deck">The good, the bad, and the better way to use customer recommendation data.</p></div><div class="hero-foot"><span>Explore the five lessons below, at your own pace.</span><span>Synthetic data throughout · Educational illustrations, not banking benchmarks</span></div></header>
<section class="author-note" aria-label="About the author"><div class="author-note-content"><div class="author-note-label">Created by</div><div class="author-note-name">David Bar-El, PhD <span>· Mixed-methods UX researcher</span></div><p>I built this guide from my own experiences with NPS over the years and conversations with other researchers and business leaders. I hope these five interactive lessons help you make better sense of NPS, question a few assumptions, and take away some practical best practices.</p></div><a class="author-note-link" href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/david-bar-el-ph-d-098bbb86/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" aria-label="Connect with David Bar-El on LinkedIn">Connect on LinkedIn <span aria-hidden="true">↗</span></a></section><nav aria-label="Jump to a lesson" class="lesson-nav"><a href="#lesson1">01 · The rise</a><a href="#lesson2">02 · What it hides</a><a href="#lesson3">03 · Context</a><a href="#lesson4">04 · Uncertainty</a><a href="#lesson5">05 · Beyond the score</a></nav>
<section class="lesson" id="lesson1"><div class="eyebrow">Lesson 01 · The rise of NPS</div><h2>How one number conquered the boardroom</h2><p class="sub">In 2003, Fred Reichheld brought NPS to a broad management audience through his <a href="https://hbr.org/2003/12/the-one-number-you-need-to-grow" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><em>Harvard Business Review</em> article, “The One Number You Need to Grow”</a>. The promise was compelling: rather than drowning in customer-satisfaction metrics, organizations could rally around one question and one memorable score.</p><ul class="argument-list"><li><strong>A remarkably simple question.</strong> Ask customers how likely they are to recommend a company to a friend or colleague, on a 0–10 scale.</li><li><strong>A number executives could understand.</strong> Subtract the percentage of detractors (0–6) from promoters (9–10). The result ranges from −100 to +100 points.</li><li><strong>A common language for the business.</strong> A single metric can travel across leadership meetings, departments, markets and reporting periods.</li><li><strong>A compelling promise.</strong> NPS was promoted not just as a measure of customer sentiment but as an indicator linked to loyalty and growth.</li><li><strong>A challenge to its bigger claims.</strong> Later research questioned whether NPS predicts business performance better than alternative customer measures, and what information gets lost along the way.</li></ul><h3 class="experiment-title">Try it yourself: How does NPS work?</h3><p class="experiment-lead">Choose a hypothetical customer population and watch how promoters, passives and detractors determine the final score.</p><div class="controls" id="l1buttons"></div><div class="cols"><div class="panel"><h3>Recommendation categories</h3><div class="bars" id="l1bar"></div><div class="legend"><span><b class="d"></b>Detractors (0–6)</span><span><b class="q"></b>Passives (7–8)</span><span><b class="p"></b>Promoters (9–10)</span></div><div id="l1numbers"></div></div><div class="panel soft"><div class="muted">THE NPS SCORE EQUALS</div><div class="big" id="l1score"></div><p id="l1formula"></p><p class="note">NPS is measured in points, ranging from −100 to +100. It is not a percentage.</p></div></div><div class="callout"><strong>Reading the calculation</strong>One memorable number makes communication easier, but promoters and detractors are the only groups that directly contribute to its calculation. Passives still matter for understanding the population.</div><div class="takeaway"><h3 class="takeaway-title">Key takeaways from Lesson 1</h3><p>The genius of NPS is its simplicity: one number can help focus an organization on its customers. But <strong>a useful management KPI is not necessarily a complete research measure.</strong> The calculation that makes NPS easy to communicate also discards information about the original responses.</p></div><p class="lesson-sources"><strong>Research behind this lesson:</strong> <a href="https://hbr.org/2003/12/the-one-number-you-need-to-grow">Reichheld (2003)</a>; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1509/jmkg.71.3.039">Keiningham et al. (2007)</a>; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1108/TQM-04-2013-0049">Kristensen &amp; Eskildsen (2014)</a>.</p><div class="lesson-bridge"><p>What if two NPS results were identical—but the customers behind them had very different experiences? Whether we compare businesses, markets, segments or moments within the same business, <strong>the same score can conceal very different realities.</strong> <a href="#lesson2">Explore Lesson 2 →</a></p></div></section>
<section class="lesson" id="lesson2"><div class="eyebrow">Lesson 02 · What the number hides</div><h2>Same NPS. Different realities.</h2><p class="sub">Imagine two customer groups reporting exactly the same NPS. On a leadership dashboard, they look identical—same KPI, perhaps even the same target achievement. But beneath the headline, their responses can tell very different stories.</p><ul class="argument-list"><li><strong>Eleven options become three categories.</strong> Scores of 0 and 6 both count as detractors, despite representing very different ratings.</li><li><strong>Identical NPS does not imply identical customers.</strong> One group can be fairly uniform while another is sharply polarized.</li><li><strong>Passives are still part of the story.</strong> Although they do not contribute directly to the NPS numerator, they can represent most of a customer group.</li><li><strong>Business decisions can differ.</strong> Two products, markets or segments with the same score may deserve different follow-up investigations.</li><li><strong>The original 0–10 distribution matters.</strong> The headline number cannot replace a view of the response shape.</li></ul><h3 class="experiment-title">Try it yourself: One score, two populations</h3><p class="experiment-lead">Start with NPS 0. Compare the groups’ response patterns and their mean recommendation ratings, then explore +20, +40 and +60.</p><div class="controls" id="l2buttons"></div><div class="cols"><div class="panel"><h3>Population A</h3><div class="big" id="l2npsA"></div><div class="hist-wrap"><div class="hist" id="histA"></div></div><div class="muted">Mean recommendation: <strong id="meanA"></strong></div></div><div class="panel"><h3>Population B</h3><div class="big" id="l2npsB"></div><div class="hist-wrap"><div class="hist" id="histB"></div></div><div class="muted">Mean recommendation: <strong id="meanB"></strong></div></div></div><div class="legend"><span><b class="d"></b>0–6</span><span><b class="q"></b>7–8</span><span><b class="p"></b>9–10</span></div><div class="callout"><strong>What changed?</strong><span id="l2explain"></span></div><p class="note">These are constructed distributions of 100 responses each, plotted on identical vertical scales. Their NPS is exact; neither distribution is sampled from real customers.</p><div class="takeaway"><h3 class="takeaway-title">Key takeaways from Lesson 2</h3><p>At NPS 0, a group in which everyone responds <strong>7</strong> looks identical on the headline KPI to a group split evenly between <strong>0 and 10</strong>. Yet the former is homogeneous and has a mean rating of 7.0, while the latter is polarized and averages 5.0.</p><p><strong>Neither NPS nor the mean alone tells the whole story.</strong> Report the original 0–10 distribution and the promoter, passive and detractor shares alongside the KPI—and investigate the reasons rather than inferring them from the shape.</p></div><p class="lesson-sources"><strong>Research behind this lesson:</strong> <a href="https://hbr.org/2003/12/the-one-number-you-need-to-grow">Reichheld (2003)</a>; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1108/TQM-04-2013-0049">Kristensen &amp; Eskildsen (2014)</a>.</p><div class="lesson-bridge"><p>But even if we preserve those responses, <strong>can we compare NPS results collected after different experiences in the customer journey?</strong> <a href="#lesson3">Explore Lesson 3 →</a></p></div></section>
<section class="lesson" id="lesson3"><div class="eyebrow">Lesson 03 · Measurement context</div><h2>Same bank. Different moments.</h2><p class="sub">Imagine you lead customer experience at a digital bank. Customers who have just set up a recurring investment report NPS +75; customers who have contacted support report −40. Does that prove investment is excellent and support is failing? <strong>Not necessarily.</strong> First, we need to know what was measured, when, and among whom.</p><ul class="argument-list"><li><strong>The moment changes the question.</strong> Evaluating an interaction immediately afterwards is different from judging your overall relationship with the bank.</li><li><strong>Transactional and relationship NPS are not interchangeable.</strong> A support-conversation survey and a bank-wide recommendation survey capture different constructs.</li><li><strong>Who is surveyed matters.</strong> People contacting support may differ systematically from those setting up investments.</li><li><strong>Wording and timing matter too.</strong> A question asked immediately after an interaction may elicit a different judgment than one asked weeks later.</li><li><strong>The survey mix can move the headline.</strong> Pooled NPS can change even when no touchpoint-level score changes.</li></ul><h3 class="experiment-title">Part A · What exactly are we measuring?</h3><p class="experiment-lead">Select a touchpoint and inspect the question. Notice how it asks about a specific event rather than the overall relationship.</p><div class="grid4" id="touchButtons"></div><div class="cols" style="margin-top:14px"><div class="panel"><div class="muted">SELECTED TOUCHPOINT NPS</div><div class="big" id="touchScore"></div><div class="bars" id="touchBar"></div><p class="note" id="touchExplain"></p></div><div class="panel soft"><div class="mini-title">Survey wording matters</div><div class="question" id="touchQuestion"></div><p class="note">The question is explicitly framed around the selected experience. This is a touchpoint evaluation, not an overall relationship measure.</p></div></div><h3>Part B · Can the overall score move when nothing improves?</h3><p class="note">These weights represent the share of surveys collected at each touchpoint. The four touchpoint scores stay fixed. The pooled score changes.</p><div class="field"><label for="mix">Survey composition</label><select id="mix"><option value="equal">Equal: 25% each</option><option value="support">Support-heavy: 60% support</option><option value="investment">Investment-heavy: 60% investment</option></select></div><div class="cols" style="margin-top:12px"><div class="stat"><div class="muted">POOLED TOUCHPOINT NPS</div><div class="big" id="pooled"></div><div class="tiny" id="mixDetail"></div></div><div class="baseline-compare"><span><strong>Equal-mix baseline</strong> +28.8</span><span><strong>Change from baseline</strong> <em id="mixDelta">0.0 pts</em></span><span><strong>Touchpoint score changes</strong> 0 pts</span></div><div class="callout" style="margin:0"><strong>What changed?</strong><span id="mixExplain"></span></div></div><p class="note">All journey distributions are hypothetical. Different scores do not establish that one team performs better than another: customer selection, survey triggers, timing and wording can all differ.</p><div class="takeaway"><h3 class="takeaway-title">Key takeaways from Lesson 3</h3><p><strong>An NPS result needs its measurement context.</strong> In this fictional example, equal-weight touchpoint surveys produce a pooled NPS of about +29. When investment surveys become more common, it rises to +53—without any touchpoint score improving.</p><p>This is a <strong>composition effect</strong>: the aggregate changes because the relative weights of its component groups change. A mathematically correct pooled score can still answer the wrong business question, particularly when the underlying surveys evaluate different experiences.</p><p>Before comparing NPS across markets, products, segments or time, check the surveyed populations, triggers, wording and collection windows. Interpret changes within comparable groups rather than relying on the pooled number alone.</p></div><p class="lesson-sources"><strong>Research behind this lesson:</strong> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1108/TQM-04-2013-0049">Kristensen &amp; Eskildsen (2014)</a> (broader measurement critique). The composition effect here is a mathematical demonstration, not an empirical finding about banks.</p><div class="lesson-bridge"><p>NPS is also tracked month after month to assess whether customer sentiment is improving or deteriorating. But when a dashboard shows a rise from <strong>+30 to +36</strong>, how confident can we be that this reflects real improvement rather than sampling variation? <a href="#lesson4">Explore Lesson 4 →</a></p></div></section>
<section class="lesson" id="lesson4"><div class="eyebrow">Lesson 04 · Tracking &amp; uncertainty</div><h2>Your NPS increased by six points. Should you celebrate?</h2><p class="sub">September’s NPS was +30. October’s is +36. The dashboard shows a green arrow; perhaps a product improvement gets the credit. But <strong>how much of that six-point movement could simply reflect which customers happened to respond?</strong></p><ul class="argument-list"><li><strong>NPS is usually an estimate, not a census.</strong> Different samples can yield different scores even if the underlying customer population is unchanged.</li><li><strong>Sample size affects precision.</strong> Small samples tend to fluctuate more, so a dashboard change may reflect sampling noise.</li><li><strong>No universal minimum n works for every NPS survey.</strong> Precision depends on sample size and the promoter/passive/detractor distribution.</li><li><strong>Equal NPS can mean unequal uncertainty.</strong> Polarized and largely passive populations can need very different samples to achieve the same margin of error.</li><li><strong>Comparing waves is a separate statistical task.</strong> We must account for uncertainty in both months, not just draw a confidence interval around one score.</li></ul><h3 class="experiment-title">Part A · How much can a sample fluctuate?</h3><p class="experiment-lead">These two hypothetical populations have the same true NPS of +30. Choose a sample size and target margin of error, then draw 20 surveys from each.</p><div class="cols"><div class="panel"><h3>Population A · Mostly passive</h3><div class="bars"><span class="q" style="width:70%"></span><span class="p" style="width:30%"></span></div><p class="tiny">30% promoters · 70% passives · 0% detractors</p><div class="big">+30</div></div><div class="panel"><h3>Population B · Polarized</h3><div class="bars"><span class="d" style="width:35%"></span><span class="p" style="width:65%"></span></div><p class="tiny">65% promoters · 0% passives · 35% detractors</p><div class="big">+30</div></div></div><div class="callout"><strong>Why does the population change the required sample size?</strong>Each promoter contributes +1, each passive 0 and each detractor −1 to the NPS calculation before multiplying by 100. Population A has many zero contributions; Population B has many opposing +1 and −1 contributions. Both average +0.30, but Population B has much greater variance. Its sample NPS therefore fluctuates more.</div><div class="field" style="margin-top:16px"><label for="sampleN">Responses per survey</label><select id="sampleN"><option>50</option><option selected="">100</option><option>200</option><option>400</option><option>1000</option></select><label for="moe">Desired 95% margin</label><select id="moe"><option value="5">±5 points</option><option selected="" value="10">±10 points</option><option value="15">±15 points</option></select></div><div class="cols" style="margin-top:12px"><div class="stat"><div class="muted">Population A · Required n</div><div class="big" id="needA"></div><div class="note" id="statusA"></div></div><div class="stat"><div class="muted">Population B · Required n</div><div class="big" id="needB"></div><div class="note" id="statusB"></div></div></div><div class="controls"><button class="primary" id="draw">↻ Draw 20 surveys from each population</button></div><div id="simulation" style="display:none"><div class="cols"><div class="panel"><div class="two"><strong>Population A</strong><span class="tiny" id="coverageA"></span></div><svg aria-label="Simulated sample NPS values for population A" id="drawA" viewbox="0 0 420 170"></svg></div><div class="panel"><div class="two"><strong>Population B</strong><span class="tiny" id="coverageB"></span></div><svg aria-label="Simulated sample NPS values for population B" id="drawB" viewbox="0 0 420 170"></svg></div></div><div class="callout"><strong>What did we learn?</strong><span id="samplingLesson"></span></div></div><p class="note">The shaded band is the chosen distance around the *known* true NPS, not a confidence interval. The count inside the band is descriptive for these 20 draws. Planning targets use the theoretical variance and a normal approximation; they do not correct for nonresponse or selection bias.</p><div class="trend-lab" id="trendLab"><h3>Part B · Is a six-point monthly increase distinguishable from noise?</h3><p>Assume two independent, comparable monthly samples, each with the stated hypothetical NPS and response proportions. Keep the observed change fixed and change how many customers responded in each month.</p><div class="field"><label for="trendN">Responses in each month</label><select id="trendN"><option value="100">100</option><option selected="" value="300">300</option><option value="1000">1,000</option><option value="3000">3,000</option></select></div><div class="cols trend-stats"><div class="stat"><div class="muted">September · NPS</div><div class="big">+30</div><p class="tiny">65% promoters · 35% detractors</p></div><div class="stat"><div class="muted">October · NPS</div><div class="big">+36</div><p class="tiny">68% promoters · 32% detractors</p></div></div><div class="trend-answer"><span class="muted">Observed change</span><strong class="trend-value">+6.0 points</strong><div class="trend-ci" id="trendCI"></div><div aria-label="Confidence interval for the NPS change; vertical mark indicates no change" class="ci-line" role="img"><div class="ci-axis" id="trendAxis"><span class="ci-zero"></span><span class="ci-range" id="trendRange"></span><span class="ci-center" id="trendCenter"></span></div><div class="two tiny"><span>−35 pts</span><span>0</span><span>+35 pts</span></div></div><p class="trend-interpretation" id="trendVerdict"></p></div><p class="note">Illustrative independent-wave normal approximation, using the separate implied category variances for +30 and +36. The interval is for the <em>difference between two estimates</em>, not the individual sample NPS. This calculation assumes comparable sampling and measurement and does not address bias or prove the cause of a change.</p></div><details><summary>Methodology appendix · Sampling assumptions and formula</summary><p>Each simulated respondent contributes X = +1, 0 or −1, with fixed probabilities. The NPS estimator is 100 × the sample mean of X. Its theoretical variance is Var(X) = p(promoter) + p(detractor) − [p(promoter) − p(detractor)]².</p><p>Approximate required n = ceiling[1.96² × 10,000 × Var(X) / desired_margin²]. Population A variance = 0.21; Population B variance = 0.91. The planning calculation assumes a 95% normal approximation and known theoretical population proportions.</p><table><tbody><tr><th>Built-in aspect</th><th>Assumption</th></tr><tr><td>Population</td><td>Fixed category proportions and true NPS +30 in both groups</td></tr><tr><td>Sampling</td><td>Independent categorical draws with replacement</td></tr><tr><td>Repetitions</td><td>20 independently simulated surveys per click and population</td></tr><tr><td>Sample size</td><td>Same user-selected n in each survey</td></tr><tr><td>Confidence</td><td>95%, z = 1.96, normal approximation</td></tr><tr><td>Precision</td><td>Selected ±5, ±10 or ±15 NPS points</td></tr><tr><td>Measurement</td><td>Category contribution +1/0/−1, not a full 0–10 score</td></tr><tr><td>Response behavior</td><td>Equal independent response probability; no nonresponse bias</td></tr><tr><td>Time</td><td>No population changes, trend or seasonality</td></tr><tr><td>Population size</td><td>Effectively unlimited; no finite-population correction</td></tr><tr><td>Design effects</td><td>No clustering, stratification or weighting</td></tr><tr><td>Question wording</td><td>No mode, wording or measurement error effects</td></tr><tr><td>Randomness</td><td>Browser pseudorandom generator; each click yields a new draw</td></tr><tr><td>Band</td><td>Selected target around true NPS; not an estimated confidence interval</td></tr><tr><td>Scope</td><td>Precision of one NPS, not power to detect a difference between waves</td></tr></tbody></table><p>In real studies, population variance is unknown and must be estimated or conservatively assumed. For published NPS confidence intervals, consider adjusted-Wald methods discussed by MeasuringU and Rocks (2016).</p></details><div class="takeaway"><h3 class="takeaway-title">Key takeaways from Lesson 4</h3><p><strong>Reported NPS is an estimate with uncertainty.</strong> At a 95% confidence level, achieving an approximate ±10-point margin of error requires about <strong>81 responses</strong> for Population A but <strong>350</strong> for Population B, despite both having true NPS +30. Their variances differ.</p><p>Larger samples improve sampling precision but do not automatically resolve nonresponse bias or inconsistent recruitment. For tracked NPS, report uncertainty and assess changes with a comparison suited to the two survey waves—rather than reading statistical significance into a dashboard arrow.</p></div><p class="lesson-sources"><strong>Research behind this lesson:</strong> <a href="https://measuringu.com/nps-ci-sample-size/">MeasuringU, sample-size planning for NPS</a>; <a href="https://measuringu.com/nps-sig-test-sample-size/">MeasuringU, comparing NPS results</a>; Rocks (2016), <em>Net Promoter Score and the Problem of Statistical Inference</em>.</p></section>
<section class="lesson" id="lesson5"><div class="eyebrow">Lesson 05 · Beyond the score</div><h2>Customers gave us a number. Now let’s listen.</h2><p class="sub">Imagine our bank has built a rigorous NPS programme. We know how customers responded, have comparable measures, and report uncertainty. But <strong>even a perfectly measured NPS does not tell us what to improve.</strong> For that, we need to understand what customers say about their experiences.</p><ul class="argument-list"><li><strong>A score tells us how customers rated—not why.</strong> Fees, reliability, support, usability and unmet expectations can all sit behind the same number.</li><li><strong>Open-ended feedback can surface unanticipated issues.</strong> Customers may raise experiences we never thought to include in a predefined survey list.</li><li><strong>Question wording shapes the responses.</strong> Asking only detractors what went wrong and only promoters what they liked makes the resulting themes harder to compare.</li><li><strong>Text can be connected to quantitative data.</strong> Coded topics let us examine what people mention and how those mentions relate to their original 0–10 rating.</li><li><strong>Association is not causation.</strong> A topic linked to a lower rating does not tell us that changing it will increase NPS.</li></ul><p class="experiment-lead">This lesson has two parts: first, design a comparable open-ended question; then explore a fictional text-informed driver analysis.</p><h3>Part A · Ask better questions, get comparable answers</h3><p>If we ask detractors what went wrong, passives what could improve, and promoters what they liked, <strong>we are steering different score groups toward different kinds of answers.</strong> Differences in the themes we uncover may therefore reflect our question wording—not simply what customers chose to share. That makes cross-score comparisons and text-informed key-driver analysis much harder to interpret.</p><p class="wording-recommendation">A better starting point: <strong>ask everyone the same neutral question: “Why did you give this score?”</strong></p><div class="wording-options" role="group" aria-label="Compare open-ended follow-up question designs"><button type="button" class="wording-option wording-option--bad" id="wordingBad" aria-pressed="false"><span class="wording-option-name">Different questions by score</span><span class="wording-option-badge">⚠ Not recommended</span></button><button type="button" class="wording-option wording-option--good active" id="wordingGood" aria-pressed="true"><span class="wording-option-name">Same question for everyone</span><span class="wording-option-badge">✓ Recommended</span></button></div><p id="wordingModeCaption" class="wording-mode-caption"></p><div class="cols wording-card-grid" id="questionCards"></div><div class="wording-impact positive" role="status" aria-live="polite"><strong id="wordingLessonTitle"></strong><span id="wordingLesson"></span></div><h3>Part B · From comments to research insights</h3><div class="two-questions"><div><strong>What are customers talking about?</strong><p>Topic frequency describes how often a theme is mentioned. It does not tell us whether the mention is praise or criticism—or how important the issue is.</p></div><div><strong>Which themes accompany higher or lower ratings?</strong><p>An adjusted statistical model examines associations with the <em>original 0–10 recommendation score</em>, accounting for other measured variables.</p></div></div><p class="note">For this exercise, a separate fictional relationship-NPS survey asks every customer the same question. Comments are coded for topics regardless of positive or negative phrasing. An OLS model adjusts for other topic mentions, customer segment and tenure; the plot shows HC3-robust 95% intervals. These are associations with the original 0–10 rating—not causal effects or changes to aggregate NPS.</p><div class="panel"><div class="two"><strong>Adjusted topic associations</strong><span class="tiny">Coefficient · 0–10 score points</span></div><div id="driverRows"></div><p class="tiny">Row label = topic · dot = adjusted association (0–10 rating points) · line = 95% interval · percentage = share mentioning the topic. Click a topic for detail.</p><div class="two tiny" style="padding-left:110px;padding-right:65px"><span>−3 lower</span><span>0</span><span>+3 higher</span></div><div class="callout"><strong id="driverTitle">Select a topic</strong><span id="driverExplain"></span></div></div><div class="cols" style="margin-top:14px"><div class="stat"><div class="muted">SYNTHETIC RESPONDENTS</div><div class="metric" id="dataN">—</div></div><div class="stat"><div class="muted">RELATIONSHIP NPS IN SYNTHETIC DATA</div><div class="metric" id="dataNPS">—</div></div></div><h3>What would you investigate first?</h3><p class="note">A larger negative coefficient does not automatically mean the largest business opportunity. Mention frequency, feasibility, cost, severity and independent behavioral evidence all matter.</p><div class="controls" id="priorityButtons"></div><div class="callout"><strong>Researcher's interpretation</strong><span id="priorityLesson"></span></div><details><summary>Methodology appendix · Text coding, modeling and limitations</summary><p>The dataset contains 1,600 wholly synthetic banking-app respondents. Every respondent is asked exactly: “What is the main reason for the score you gave?” The generator produces one or two short fictional statements from a predefined phrase bank. Transparent rule-based topic indicators are stored as <code>topic_*</code> columns. A response can contain more than one topic. A topic is coded when mentioned regardless of whether the phrase praises or criticizes it.</p><p>The model is ordinary least squares: recommendation_score ~ seven topic indicators + customer segment + tenure. HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors produce the plotted intervals. The 0–10 score—not an invented individual NPS—is the outcome. The R script independently fits the same specification.</p><p>Crucially, the synthetic data were generated with deliberately designed experience–score relationships, including noise. The displayed coefficients are estimated from that dataset; they are not empirical banking findings or evidence of causal effects. Topic mentions are endogenous to respondents' chosen explanations, non-mentions do not mean an experience was absent, and short phrases do not capture full qualitative nuance. The model adjusts for listed predictors only. Correlated topics, omitted factors, imperfect coding, respondent selection and score-conditioned explanations can distort interpretation. The model's coefficient does not predict how much NPS would change after an intervention. Human review and validation of text coding are required in a real study.</p></details><div class="takeaway"><h3 class="takeaway-title">Key takeaways from Lesson 5</h3><p><strong>Customer feedback is most useful when we connect what people say to how they rate—but never treat either as sufficient on its own.</strong> A common topic is not necessarily the most important business priority; a statistical association does not establish an effective intervention.</p><p>Use open-ended answers to discover experiences, quantitative analysis to identify patterns worth investigating, and further research or experimentation to test potential remedies. The result is not a guaranteed recipe for increasing NPS, but <strong>a more evidence-led starting point for action.</strong></p></div><p class="lesson-sources"><strong>Methods and further reading:</strong> <a href="https://www.tidytextmining.com/">Silge &amp; Robinson, <em>Text Mining with R</em></a>; <a href="https://measuringu.com/key-drivers/">MeasuringU, key-driver analysis</a>. These sources inform methods; the results below are derived solely from fabricated data.</p></section>
<section class="lesson"><div class="eyebrow">Putting it together</div><h2>Five habits of a better NPS programme</h2><p class="sub">You can keep the KPI and still be a more critical researcher. A practical programme pairs the simplicity of NPS with evidence that makes the number interpretable and actionable.</p><ol class="habits"><li><strong>Keep the headline, preserve the detail.</strong> Report the full 0–10 distribution and category shares, not just the final score.</li><li><strong>Compare like with like.</strong> Distinguish relationship from transactional measures; document survey triggers, timing, questions and population mix.</li><li><strong>Report uncertainty.</strong> Match sample planning to expected variance, and test changes across waves rather than celebrating arrows.</li><li><strong>Ask the same neutral “why” question.</strong> Invite comparable, open-ended explanations and review the resulting text for nuance.</li><li><strong>Turn associations into investigations.</strong> Combine topic frequency, modeled patterns and other evidence; validate proposed improvements before claiming causal impact.</li></ol><p class="ending-line">NPS can start a conversation. Good research is what moves the conversation forward.</p><details class="reading"><summary>References and further reading</summary><ol class="reading-list"><li>Reichheld, F. F.
